claim: Ctenophora has recently emerged as one of the earliest-branching extant animal phyla.
source: Ctenophora has recently emerged as one of the earliest-branching extant phyla (Ryan et al., 2013; Moroz et al., 2014; Whelan et al., 2015; Telford et al., 2016), along with the sponges (Porifera) (Pisani et al., 2015; Jékely et al., 2015; Telford et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: The basement membrane is a hallmark morphological feature of the microenvironment of epithelial tissues.
source: The basement membrane (BM), a specialized form of extracellular matrix (ECM), is a hallmark morphological feature of the microenvironment of epithelial tissues, and its appearance within the non-bilaterian animal phyla suggests it was a prerequisite (Sherwood, 2015; Hynes, 2012; Ozbek et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: The basement membrane has numerous functions including maintaining tissue architecture and compartmentalization.
source: The BM has numerous functions including maintaining tissue architecture and compartmentalization, organizing growth factor signaling gradients, guiding cell migration and adhesion, delineating apical-basal polarity modulating cell differentiation during development, orchestrating cell behavior in tissue repair after injury, and guiding organ regeneration (Hynes, 2009; Yurchenco, 2011; Vracko, 1974; Pöschl et al., 2004; Daley and Yamada, 2013; Wang et al., 2008; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Song and Ott, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Systematic assessment by electron microscopy of Mnemiopsis revealed no organized basement membrane.
source: Systematic assessment by EM of a number of sections from similar areas in Mnemiopsis was conducted, and no organized basement membrane was encountered.
evidence: Based on electron microscopy observations reported in the manuscript

claim: Tight junctions between cells and cellular polarization were not observed in Mnemiopsis.
source: Furthermore, tight junctions between cells and cellular polarization were not observed, both hallmarks of epithelial basement membrane tissue structure (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy observations and reference to Figure 1B

claim: In Beroe and Pleurobrachia, electron microscopy indicated an electron dense layer underlying cells along with cell polarization and lateral tight junctions between cells.
source: In Beroe and Pleurobrachia, however, EM indicated an electron dense layer underlying cells along with cell polarization, and lateral tight junctions between cells, and IHC similarly showed a dense collagen IV layer underlying cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry observations with reference to Figure 1B

claim: The features observed in Beroe and Pleurobrachia are congruent with basement membrane architecture and epithelial tissue.
source: Together, these features are congruent with basement membrane architecture and epithelial tissue.
evidence: Inference based on the observed structural features

claim: Nematostella demonstrated presence of basement membrane, characterized by polarized cells apical to an electron dense layer by EM.
source: Nematostella demonstrated presence of basement membrane, characterized by polarized cells apical to an electron dense layer by EM, and a concentrated region of collagen IV underlying cell nuclei by IHC (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry observations with reference to Figure 1C

claim: Ctenophora revealed a simplified set of ECM proteins, with collagen IV and laminin as the only components identified across Beroe, Pleurobrachia, and Mnemiopsis.
source: Ctenophora, however, revealed a simplified set of ECM proteins, with collagen IV and laminin as the only components identified across Beroe, Pleurobrachia, and Mnemiopsis (Figure 1B and Figure 2).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic and genomic analysis with reference to Figures 1B and 2

claim: Despite lacking the full gamut of bilaterian ECM proteins, ctenophore cells can still construct a prototypical basement membrane in Pleurobrachia and Beroe.
source: Importantly, despite lacking the full gamut of bilaterian ECM proteins, ctenophore cells can still construct a prototypical basement membrane in Pleurobrachia and Beroe.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations and ECM composition analysis

claim: Mnemiopsis does not form a basement membrane despite exhibiting the very same toolkit proteins, which may be a result of secondary loss event.
source: Mnemiopsis, however, does not form a BM despite exhibiting the very same toolkit proteins and this may be a result of secondary loss event.
evidence: Observation combined with speculative reasoning about evolutionary loss

claim: Placozoa and the poriferan classes of calcareous and demosponges lack basement membranes.
source: Placozoa and the poriferan classes of calcareous and demosponges lack basement membranes (Figure 1C) (Ozbek et al., 2010; Leys et al., 2009; Ruthmann et al., 1986; Srivastava et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1C

claim: The absence of basement membranes in some lineages suggests the BM may have been secondarily lost or is present only at specific stages during their life cycle.
source: suggesting the BM may have been secondarily lost in these lineages (Cock, 2010) or that it is present only at specific stages during their life cycle (Hynes, 2012).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations

claim: Placozoa contains the necessary components for a BM, including collagen IV, laminin, perlecan, and nidogen.
source: Specifically, Placozoa contains the necessary components for a BM, including collagen IV, laminin, perlecan, and nidogen (Srivastava et al., 2008) and also exhibits spongin (Figure 1C and Figure 2) (vide infra).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figures 1C and 2

claim: The ECM of homoscleromorph sponges contains basement membranes with collagen IV and laminin, but no spongin.
source: In Porifera, the ECM of homoscleromorph sponges contains basement membranes (Boute et al., 1996), with collagen IV and laminin, but no spongin (Figure 1C and Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figures 1C and 2

claim: Demosponges lack any detectable collagen IV and only contain laminin-related domains and spongin.
source: Demosponges, on the other hand, lack any detectable collagen IV and only contain laminin-related domains and spongin.
evidence: Based on genomic and transcriptomic analysis

claim: The Demosponge and Hexactinellidae classes of Porifera, which both lack collagen IV, do not have basement membranes.
source: In contrast, the Demosponge and Hexactinellidae classes of Porifera, which both lack collagen IV, do not have basement membranes (Figure 1C) (Adams et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1C

claim: Laminin architecture appears to be present in choanoflagellates.
source: Laminin architecture appears to be present in choanoflagellates (Fahey and Degnan, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: No other complete ECM components exist in unicellular choanoflagellates, but several domains and fragments of ECM components have been identified.
source: Although no other complete ECM components exist in unicellular choanoflagellates (King, 2005), several domains and fragments of ECM components have been identified, including collagenous repeats, laminin G (globular) domains and LN (N-terminal) domains, and fibronectin type II and III domains (Figure 1D) (King et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1D

claim: Collagen IV is absent in unicellular sister-groups.
source: Moreover, collagen IV is absent in unicellular sister-groups.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: In Mnemiopsis, 11 full-length collagen IV genes were discovered.
source: In Mnemiopsis, 11 full-length collagen IV genes were discovered, which contrasts with the two genes typically present throughout invertebrates and the six genes typically found in vertebrates (Khoshnoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with citation for comparison

claim: Four Mnemiopsis collagen IV genes occur on the same scaffold and exhibit a head-to-head orientation.
source: In Mnemiopsis, four genes occur on the same scaffold and exhibit a head-to-head orientation (ML17501a and ML17504a, ML17502a and ML17503a) (designated as Group I) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3A

claim: The head-to-head orientation is a distinguishing characteristic of collagen IV genes among other collagens of Bilateria.
source: The head-to-head orientation is a distinguishing characteristic of collagen IV genes among other collagens of Bilateria (Kaytes et al., 1988; Hudson et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of adult Mnemiopsis reveals differential expression within each group of collagen IV genes.
source: Transcriptomic analysis of adult Mnemiopsis reveals differential expression within each group of collagen IV genes.
evidence: Based on transcriptomic analysis

claim: Mnemiopsis collagen IV genes are shorter in sequence length and typically have fewer exons and shorter intronic regions compared to their Bilaterian counterparts.
source: Mnemiopsis collagen IV genes are shorter in sequence length and typically have fewer exons and shorter intronic regions compared to their Bilaterian counterparts (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3C

claim: Across ten ctenophore species, a total of 118 unique collagen IV genes were detected.
source: Across these ten species, a total of 118 unique collagen IV genes were detected.
evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis

claim: Each ctenophore species contained a variable number of collagen IV genes, ranging between 4 and 20 genes each.
source: Each species contained a variable number of collagen IV genes, ranging between 4 and 20 genes each, as compared to the 2 to 6 genes in the other non-bilaterian animal phyla and Bilateria (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis with reference to Figures 4A and B

claim: In addition to full-length collagen IV genes, two genes encoding only the NC1 domain were identified across ten species of Ctenophora.
source: In addition to full-length collagen IV genes, two genes, with signal peptides, encoding only the NC1 domain were identified across ten species of Ctenophora.
evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis

claim: Expression of NC1 domains without collagenous tails is novel.
source: Expression of NC1 domains without collagenous tails is novel (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with other organisms and reference to Figure 4C

claim: Two collagen IV genes were found in both Nematostella vectensis and Trichoplax adhaerens, demonstrating a 'head-to-head' orientation.
source: We found two genes in both species, and that they are homologous with Bilateria, with each demonstrating a 'head-to-head' orientation and homologous coding regions for both collagenous and non-collagenous domains (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3D

claim: Unicellular protists do not contain collagen IV as determined by genomic analyses.
source: In contrast, unicellular protists (Choanozoa, Filasterea, Amoebozoa, Apusozoa) do not contain collagen IV as determined by genomic analyses (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 2

claim: Head-to-head orientation of collagen IV is conserved across Bilateria, Cnidaria, Placozoa, and Ctenophora.
source: Together, our findings show that head-to-head orientation of collagen IV is conserved across Bilateria, Cnidaria, Placozoa, and Ctenophora, whereas Ctenophora exhibits both head-to-head and tandem orientations (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Structural domains of collagen IV including NC3, collagenous domain, and NC1 domain are conserved across Cnidaria, Placozoa, Porifera, and Ctenophora.
source: Indeed, these domains are conserved across Cnidaria, Placozoa, Porifera, and Ctenophora (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis with reference to Figure 5

claim: The chloride-binding motif was identified in both Ctenophora (group II chains) as well as in the two Homoscleromorph sponges analyzed.
source: The chloride-binding motif was identified in both Ctenophora (group II chains) as well as in the two Homoscleromorph sponges analyzed, suggesting the chloride signaling function of NC1 domains is also conserved in Ctenophora and Porifera (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Sulfilimine cross-links are conserved throughout Bilateria, from Humans to C. elegans, and in Cnidaria, with the exception of Hydra.
source: Sulfilimine cross-links are conserved throughout Bilateria, from Humans to C. elegans, and in Cnidaria, with the exception of Hydra (Fidler et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Sulfilimine cross-links are absent in Ctenophora, owing to the absence of Met-93 and Lys/Hyl-211 residues.
source: In contrast, this cross-link is absent in Ctenophora, owing to the absence of Met-93 and Lys/Hyl-211 residues (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: Ctenophore collagen IV is distinguished from all other metazoans by the presence of two additional domains: an NC2 domain and a cysteine-loop.
source: Uniquely, ctenophore collagen IV is distinguished from all other metazoans by the presence of two additional domains. One is a non-collagenous domain (NC2 domain) that is approximately 38–44 residues in length within the collagenous domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 5). The other domain is 11–13 residues in length and consists of 3–4 conserved cysteine residues, designated as the cysteine-loop, which is an extension of the canonical NC1 domain, and a candidate for an alternative cross-linking mechanism (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6

claim: Analysis in the three ctenophore species, Mnemiopsis, Beroe and Pleurobrachia, revealed the presence of NC1 hexamers, which upon reduction dissociated into dimers.
source: Analysis in the three ctenophore species, Mnemiopsis, Beroe and Pleurobrachia, by SDS-PAGE and gel filtration chromatography, revealed the presence of NC1 hexamers, which upon reduction dissociated into dimers (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Based on biochemical analysis with reference to Figures 7A-D

claim: Ctenophore dimers are stabilized by the cysteine-loop.
source: Since the dimers lack Met-93 and Lys/Hyl-211, the results indicate that ctenophore dimers are stabilized by the cysteine-loop (Figure 7E).
evidence: Inference based on biochemical analysis and sequence data with reference to Figure 7E

claim: The cross-linking mechanism of ctenophores (cysteine-loop) is distinguished from that of Cnidaria and Bilateria (sulfilimine cross-links).
source: Hence, the cross-linking mechanism of ctenophores (cysteine-loop) is distinguished from that of Cnidaria and Bilateria (sulfilimine cross-links).
evidence: Inference based on biochemical and sequence analysis

claim: All 10 ctenophore species possess a gene encoding only the NC1 domain, a feature not found in any other phyla.
source: Uniquely, all 10 ctenophore species possess a gene encoding only the NC1 domain, a feature not found in any other phyla.
evidence: Based on transcriptomic analysis

claim: Phylogenetic analysis placed the NC1 domain of ctenophore collagen IV into two major groups, which are consistent with genomic orientation of Group I and Group II.
source: The results placed the NC1 domain of ctenophore collagen IV into two major groups, which are consistent with genomic orientation of Group I and Group II (vida supra).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Group I and Group II ctenophore chains showed a much higher rate of divergence both within the phylum and as compared to the other non-bilaterian animal phyla and bilaterian collagen IV sequences.
source: Furthermore, Group I and Group II ctenophore chains showed a much higher rate of divergence both within the phylum and as compared to the other non-bilaterian animal phyla and bilaterian collagen IV sequences.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Spongins are a family of collagen IV-related proteins composed of a short collagenous domain attached to an NC1 domain.
source: Spongins are a family of collagen IV-related proteins composed of a short collagenous domain attached to an NC1 domain.
evidence: Based on structural analysis

claim: Spongins were first detected in the exoskeleton of demosponges and have been subsequently identified in cnidarians, across invertebrates (with the exception of ecdysozoans), and in basal chordates.
source: This protein family was first detected in the exoskeleton of demosponges and has been subsequently identified in cnidarians, across invertebrates (with the exception of ecdysozoans, e.g., C. elegans, Drosophila), and in basal chordates (Aouacheria et al., 2006; Exposito et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Spongins do not occur in vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, spongins do not occur in vertebrates (Aouacheria et al., 2006), and we did not detect them in Ctenophora.
evidence: Supported by citation and genomic analysis

claim: Multiple sequence alignment showed conservation of seven cysteine residues between spongins and collagen IV.
source: Multiple sequence alignment showed conservation of seven cysteine residues between spongins and collagen IV, while the HSQ motif was absent in spongin sequences (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment with reference to Figure 9

claim: The presence of collagenous domains and the conservation of collagen IV NC1 domain features within spongin NC1 domains reveal that they are homologous to collagen IV protein domain structure.
source: Collectively, the presence of collagenous domains and the conservation of collagen IV NC1 domain features within spongin NC1 domains, reveal that they are homologous to collagen IV protein domain structure, as previously noted (Exposito et al., 1991).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and supported by citation

claim: Within Ctenophora, collagen IV underwent numerous gene duplication events resulting in an unprecedented diversity in both gene sequence and organization in comparison to all other metazoans.
source: Within Ctenophora, collagen IV underwent numerous gene duplication events resulting in an unprecedented diversity in both gene sequence and organization in comparison to all other metazoans.
evidence: Based on genomic and transcriptomic analysis

claim: Collagen IV genes are highly conserved across the non-bilaterian animal phyla and Bilateria; yet, in Ctenophora, these genes are more diverse and distinct including a novel cross-linking mechanism, with up to 20 distinct genes compared with six in vertebrates.
source: Collectively, collagen IV genes are highly conserved across the non-bilaterian animal phyla and Bilateria; yet, in Ctenophora, these genes are more diverse and distinct including a novel cross-linking mechanism, with up to 20 distinct genes compared with six in vertebrates.
evidence: Based on genomic and biochemical analysis

claim: The collagen IV gene is absent in the unicellular sister-groups (choanoflagellates, filastereans, amoebozoans, and apusozoans), suggesting it was an early metazoan innovation.
source: Moreover, the collagen IV gene is absent in the unicellular sister-groups (choanoflagellates, filastereans, amoebozoans, and apusozoans), suggesting it was an early metazoan innovation.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with inference about evolutionary origin

claim: In both Ctenophora-first and Porifera-first scenarios, collagen IV appeared in an early metazoan ancestor or a unicellular ancestor but was secondarily lost in demosponges and hexactinellid sponges.
source: In both scenarios, collagen IV appeared in an early metazoan ancestor or a unicellular ancestor but was secondarily lost in demosponges and hexactinellid sponges (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic analysis with reference to Figures 10A and B

claim: The NC1 gene is present only in Ctenophora, suggesting that this gene is a remnant from an early metazoan ancestor, and a forerunner to the NC1 domain of the ancestral collagen IV gene.
source: It is noteworthy that the NC1 gene is present only in Ctenophora (Figure 10C and D), suggesting that this gene is a remnant from an early metazoan ancestor, and a forerunner to the NC1 domain of the ancestral collagen IV gene.
evidence: Inference based on genomic analysis with reference to Figures 10C and D

claim: The presence of Gly-X-Y collagenous repeats in choanoflagellates and amoebozoa, and the presence of a NC1 gene in the Ctenophora phylum suggests that Gly-X-Y repeats combined with an NC1 domain gene in an early metazoan ancestor, or possibly in a unicellular ancestor, forming an ancestral collagen IV gene.
source: The presence of Gly-X-Y collagenous repeats, in the absence of a collagen IV gene, in choanoflagellates and amoebozoa, and the presence of a NC1 gene in the Ctenophora phylum suggests that Gly-X-Y repeats combined with an NC1 domain gene in an early metazoan ancestor, or possibly in a unicellular ancestor, forming an ancestral collagen IV gene.
evidence: Inference based on genomic analysis and evolutionary reasoning

claim: Collagen IV protein, or its spongin variant, is a required ECM component for all extant multicellular animals.
source: Collagen IV protein, or its spongin variant, is a required ECM component for all extant multicellular animals, considering that all animals investigated contain either collagen IV or spongin, and that the essentiality of collagen IV during development has been established in several studies (Gupta et al., 1997; Pöschl et al., 2004; Gotenstein et al., 2010; Bhave et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis and supported by citations

claim: The collagen IV protein is associated with two distinct organizations of cells: one in which the ECM contains collagen IV broadly dispersed between communities of cells (Mnemiopsis) and the other in which collagen IV is a component of a well-defined BM underlying a layer of cells (Beroe, Pleurobrachia, Homoscleromorph sponges, and Nematostella).
source: The collagen IV protein is associated with two distinct organizations of cells; one in which the ECM contains collagen IV broadly dispersed between communities of cells (Mnemiopsis) and the other in which collagen IV is a component of a well-defined BM underlying a layer of cells (Beroe, Pleurobrachia, Homoscleromorph sponges, and Nematostella), a hallmark feature of epithelial bilaterian tissues (Figure 12).
evidence: Based on structural observations with reference to Figure 12

claim: The absence of BMs in Trichoplax and Mnemiopsis suggests there is an unknown component that facilitates the assembly of collagen IV and laminin into a basement membrane.
source: The absence of BMs in Trichoplax and Mnemiopsis suggests there is an unknown component that facilitates the assembly of collagen IV and laminin into a basement membrane.
evidence: Inference based on observations of ECM composition and structure

claim: Collagen IV and its spongin variant are primordial components of the extracellular microenvironment.
source: Collectively, we conclude that collagen IV and its spongin variant are primordial components of the extracellular microenvironment, and collagen IV, as a component of BM, enabled the assembly of a fundamental architectural unit for the genesis and evolution of multicellular tissues (Figure 12).
evidence: Conclusion based on all analyses with reference to Figure 12

claim: Collagen IV, as a component of BM, enabled the assembly of a fundamental architectural unit for the genesis and evolution of multicellular tissues.
source: Collectively, we conclude that collagen IV and its spongin variant are primordial components of the extracellular microenvironment, and collagen IV, as a component of BM, enabled the assembly of a fundamental architectural unit for the genesis and evolution of multicellular tissues (Figure 12).
evidence: Conclusion based on all analyses with reference to Figure 12

claim: The fundamental architectural unit is characterized by a layer of apical/basal-polarized cells that are laterally connected by tight junctions between plasma membranes, which are basally anchored via integrin receptors embedded in plasma membranes to a basement membrane supra-scaffold.
source: This unit is characterized by a layer of apical/basal-polarized cells that are laterally connected by tight junctions between plasma membranes, which are basally anchored via integrin receptors embedded in plasma membranes to a basement membrane supra-scaffold.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations and knowledge of tissue architecture

claim: This architectural unit served as the building block that enabled the formation and evolution of epithelial tissues, the ever-increasing complexity and size of organisms, and for the expansion and diversity of the animal kingdom.
source: In turn, this architectural unit served as the building block that enabled the formation and evolution of epithelial tissues, the ever-increasing complexity and size of organisms, and for the expansion and diversity of the animal kingdom.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary reasoning

claim: Collagen IV is an ancient protein with up to six distinct genes (COL4A1, COL4A2, COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5, COL4A6), essential for early development.
source: Among these proteins, recent studies reveal collagen IV is an ancient protein with up to six distinct genes (COL4A1, COL4A2, COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5, COL4A6), essential for early development, that functions as a smart scaffold providing tensile strength to tissues, influencing cell behavior by tethering diverse macromolecules, including laminin, proteoglycans, growth factors, binding integrins (Gupta et al., 1997; Bhave et al., 2012; McCall et al., 2014; Fidler et al., 2014; Pöschl et al., 2004; Vanacore et al., 2009; Cummings et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2008; Parkin et al., 2011; Emsley et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Disrupting collagen IV scaffolds causes BM destabilization and tissue dysfunction in mice, zebrafish, flies, and nematodes.
source: Disrupting collagen IV scaffolds causes BM destabilization and tissue dysfunction in mice, zebrafish, flies, and nematodes (Pöschl et al., 2004; Fidler et al., 2014; Borchiellini et al., 1996; Gupta et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The NC1 domain is the molecular recognition module that directs the assembly of collagen IV protomers and networks.
source: The NC1 domain is the molecular recognition module that directs the assembly of collagen IV protomers and networks (Cummings et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: NC1 modules function in selecting collagen IV chains for trimerization, forming triple-helical protomers, and for oligomerization of protomers into networks.
source: NC1 modules function in selecting collagen IV chains for trimerization, forming triple-helical protomers, and for oligomerization of protomers into networks (Figure 5) (Cummings et al., 2016; Khoshnoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations with reference to Figure 5

claim: The NC1 modules are stabilized by sulfilimine cross-links, which connect methionine-93 (Met-93) and lysine/hydroxylysine-211 (Lys/Hyl-211) between adjoining protomers.
source: The NC1 modules are stabilized by sulfilimine cross-links, which connect methionine-93 (Met-93) and lysine/hydroxylysine-211 (Lys/Hyl-211) between adjoining protomers (Fidler et al., 2014; Vanacore et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The basement membrane is a supramolecular scaffold, comprised of a toolkit of proteins including collagen IV, laminin, perlecan, and nidogen.
source: The basement membrane is a supramolecular scaffold, comprised of a toolkit of proteins including collagen IV, laminin, perlecan, and nidogen (Hynes, 2012; Fahey and Degnan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The ECM components in Nematostella are very similar to that of most bilaterian species BMs, including human, mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans.
source: The ECM components in Nematostella are very similar to that of most bilaterian species BMs (Hynes, 2012), including human, mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, consisting of collagen IV, laminin, peroxidasin, collagen XV and XVIII, perlecan, nidogen, fibronectin, as well as spongin (Figure 1C and Figure 2).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with citation and reference to Figures 1C and 2

claim: Immunohistochemistry was congruent with electron microscopy findings in Mnemiopsis, indicating that collagen IV was dispersed throughout the tissue, surrounding and encompassing cells.
source: IHC was congruent with this finding, indicating that collagen IV was dispersed throughout the tissue, surrounding and encompassing cells.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry observations

claim: Nematostella has a bilayer body structure composed of endoderm and ectoderm layer with an intervening mesoglea.
source: Nematostella, along with other cnidarians, have a bilayer body structure composed of endoderm and ectoderm layer with an intervening mesoglea; however, the general BM structure is congruent with that of bilaterian organisms, including mammals.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cnidarian anatomy

claim: The general BM structure in Nematostella is congruent with that of bilaterian organisms, including mammals.
source: Nematostella, along with other cnidarians, have a bilayer body structure composed of endoderm and ectoderm layer with an intervening mesoglea; however, the general BM structure is congruent with that of bilaterian organisms, including mammals.
evidence: Based on structural observations

claim: Basement membranes are uncommon across Porifera and Placozoa.
source: Across Porifera and Placozoa, basement membranes are uncommon.
evidence: Based on structural observations

claim: Basement membranes may have independently evolved in Ctenophora, Porifera, and Bilateria.
source: Alternatively, basement membranes may have independently evolved in Ctenophora, Porifera, and Bilateria, a phenomenon that could have occurred because of shared inheritance of ECM proteins and domains from the last common ancestor of the non-bilaterian animal phyla.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observations

claim: Many of the BM toolkit components are present in the non-bilaterian animal phyla.
source: Investigation of the non-bilaterian animal phyla for components of the BM toolkit suggests that many of the components are present (Srivastava et al., 2010, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Laminin-related genes appear in all unicellular species including Capsaspora owczarzaki, Dictyostelium discoideum, and Thecamonas trahens.
source: Laminin architecture appears to be present in choanoflagellates (Fahey and Degnan, 2012), and additionally laminin-related genes appear in all other unicellular species including Capsaspora owczarzaki, Dictyostelium discoideum, and Thecamonas trahens (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with citation and reference to Figure 2

claim: Collagenous GXY repeats were identified in Monosiga, Salpingoeca, and Dictyostelium.
source: Furthermore, no other complete ECM components exist in other unicellular organisms, including Salpingoeca rosetta (Choanozoa), Capsaspora owczarzaki (Filasterea), Dictyostelium discoideum (Amoebozoa), or Thecamonas trahens (Apusozoa); however, collagenous GXY repeats were identified in Monosiga, Salpingoeca, and Dictyostelium.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: Integrins are highly conserved across metazoa and are found in the unicellular Capsaspora and Thecamonas.
source: Integrins are highly conserved across metazoa and are found in the unicellular Capsaspora and Thecamonas.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: Dystrophin was identified in humans, fruit fly, Nematostella, Amphimedon, as well as in unicellular protists but is absent in Trichoplax, Oscarella, and ctenophores.
source: Dystrophin was identified in humans, fruit fly, Nematostella, Amphimedon, as well as in unicellular protists but is absent in Trichoplax, Oscarella, and ctenophores.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: DDR 1 and 2 was identified only in humans and fruit fly.
source: DDR 1 and 2 was identified only in humans and fruit fly.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: The ECM composition across the non-bilaterian animal phyla points to laminin and collagen IV as highly conserved components associated with BM and epithelial tissue architecture.
source: Collectively, the ECM composition across the non-bilaterian animal phyla points to laminin and collagen IV as highly conserved components, and importantly, that they are associated with BM and epithelial tissue architecture.
evidence: Inference based on genomic and structural analysis

claim: In Group I of Mnemiopsis collagen IV genes, the expression of ML17501a and ML17502a is significantly higher than other Group I genes.
source: In Group I, the expression of ML17501a and ML17502a is significantly higher than other Group I genes.
evidence: Based on transcriptomic analysis

claim: ML034334a, ML0343336a, and ML0343337a show considerable increase in expression levels compared to the other Group II genes in Mnemiopsis.
source: Similarly, ML034334a, ML0343336a, and ML0343337a show considerable increase in expression levels compared to the other Group II genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic analysis with reference to Figure 3B

claim: Bilaterian fibrillar collagen genes are composed of multiple exons with a length of 54 base pairs.
source: Whereas bilaterian fibrillar collagen genes are composed of multiple exons with a length of 54 base pairs (Yamada et al., 1980), exons of Mnemiopsis collagen IV genes range in size from 40 to 4867 bp.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The presence of split glycine codons coding for the collagenous domain and codons on junctional exons are defining features of vertebrate collagen IV genes.
source: The presence of split glycine codons coding for the collagenous domain and codons on junctional exons (e.g. collagenous domain/NC1 domain encoding exons) are defining features of vertebrate collagen IV genes (Quinones et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Multiple Mnemiopsis genes from each group possess split glycine codons on the collagenous domain/NC1 domain junction exon.
source: Multiple genes from each group (Group I: ML17501a, ML17502a, and ML17503a; Group II: ML034334a, ML034336a, and ML034337a) possess split glycine codons on the collagenous domain/NC1 domain junction exon (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: All ctenophore species contain a combination of both Group I and II chains, with the exception of the two Beroe species which exhibit only Group II chains.
source: All species, apart from the two Beroe species surveyed, contain a combination of both Group I and II chains, with the two Beroe species exhibiting only Group II chains.
evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis

claim: Putative signal peptides were detected in at least three ctenophore NC1 genes.
source: Putative signal peptides were detected in at least three ctenophore NC1 genes, Mnemiopsis (ml047918a), Pleurobrachia pileus (pp_COL4_i), and Pleurobrachia bachei (PBNC1_1) based on SignalP prediction (http://www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/SignalP/).
evidence: Based on computational prediction

claim: The chloride-binding motif functions in binding extracellular chloride to signal the assembly of collagen IV networks and is conserved from vertebrates to Cnidaria and Placozoa.
source: The NC1 domain also contains a chloride-binding motif, which functions in binding extracellular chloride to signal the assembly of collagen IV networks and is conserved from vertebrates to Cnidaria and Placozoa (Cummings et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The chloride signaling function of NC1 domains is conserved in Ctenophora and Porifera.
source: The chloride-binding motif was identified in both Ctenophora (group II chains) as well as in the two Homoscleromorph sponges analyzed, suggesting the chloride signaling function of NC1 domains is also conserved in Ctenophora and Porifera (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inference based on sequence analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The conserved structural features of bilaterian collagen IV extend across the non-bilaterian animal phyla, including Ctenophora.
source: Together, these findings reveal that the conserved structural features of bilaterian collagen IV extend across the non-bilaterian animal phyla, including Ctenophora.

claim: RAxML phylogenetic analysis revealed a closer affinity between the ctenophore NC1 genes and collagen IV NC1 domain from the non-bilaterian animal phyla and Bilateria, as compared to ctenophore Group I and II chains.

claim: The unrooted tree topology illustrates the high phylogenetic affinity between ctenophore NC1 proteins and bilaterian NC1 domain that cluster closely.

source: Comparison of collagen IV sequences revealed four cysteine residues that are absent in spongin sequences.

claim: The essentiality of collagen IV during development has been established in several studies.
source: Collagen IV protein, or its spongin variant, is a required ECM component for all extant multicellular animals, considering that all animals investigated contain either collagen IV or spongin, and that the essentiality of collagen IV during development has been established in several studies (Gupta et al., 1997; Pöschl et al., 2004; Gotenstein et al., 2010; Bhave et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations
